q: Iodine (I₂) is a non-polar molecule. It dissolves best in:
x: "Like dissolves like": non-polar I₂ dissolves in non-polar CCl₄. It is only very slightly soluble in polar water and in aqueous solutions.

q: According to kinetic molecular theory, diffusion is much slower in liquids than in gases because liquid molecules:
o: Are close together and attract each other, with little free space to move in
Are much heavier than gas molecules
Move only in straight lines without collisions
x: Liquid molecules are always moving, but they are packed closely and held by intermolecular forces, so they collide constantly and travel only short distances. Gas molecules have large empty spaces and weak attractions, so they spread out quickly.

q: Which property distinguishes a crystalline solid from an amorphous solid?
o: It softens gradually over a range of temperature
It melts sharply at a definite temperature
Its particles have no regular arrangement
It behaves like a supercooled liquid
x: Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating arrangement of particles, so all bonds break at one temperature and they melt sharply. Amorphous solids such as glass soften over a range of temperature.

q: In the sodium chloride crystal, the Cl⁻ ions (and likewise the Na⁺ ions) are arranged in a:
x: NaCl has a face-centred cubic arrangement: each set of ions forms an fcc lattice, and each ion sits at the centre of an octahedron of six oppositely charged ions.

q: Sodium chloride dissolves in water but not in benzene because:
o: Water molecules are polar and attract and surround the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
x: The negative (oxygen) end of water dipoles attracts Na⁺ and the positive (hydrogen) end attracts Cl⁻, pulling ions out of the lattice. Non-polar benzene cannot attract ions in this way.

q: Liquids are almost incompressible because:
o: There is very little empty space between their molecules
Their molecules have no kinetic energy
Their molecules repel each other strongly at all distances
x: Liquid molecules are already very close to one another, so pressure can push them only slightly closer. Gases are easily compressed because most of their volume is empty space.

q: A crystal shows different values of refractive index and electrical conductivity when measured in different directions. This property is called:
x: Anisotropy means physical properties depend on direction, because the arrangement of particles differs along different axes of a crystal. Isotropic substances, such as amorphous solids, have the same properties in all directions.

q: The smallest part of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in three dimensions, generates the whole lattice is called the:
x: The unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice. Lattice points are the positions occupied by particles; habit and cleavage describe the outer shape and breaking of the crystal.

q: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane (C₆H₁₄) does not. This is because:
o: Hexane is polar and water is non-polar
Hexane has a lower molar mass than ethanol
Ethanol's polar O–H group can form hydrogen bonds with water, while hexane is non-polar
x: Ethanol has a polar O–H group that hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so it mixes. Hexane is non-polar and cannot attract water molecules, so the two form separate layers.

q: A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. In terms of kinetic molecular theory, this is because its molecules:
o: Are fixed in definite positions in a lattice
Are far apart and move freely in all directions
Are held close by intermolecular forces but can slide past one another
Have no attractive forces between them
x: Intermolecular forces keep liquid molecules close, fixing the volume, but the molecules are not locked in place, so the liquid can flow and take any shape. Fixed lattice positions describe solids; free, distant molecules describe gases.

q: Which pair of substances is isomorphous?
x: Isomorphous substances are different compounds with the same crystal form; NaNO₃ and CaCO₃ both crystallise in the same (rhombohedral) form with the same atomic ratio 1 : 1 : 3. Diamond/graphite and the two sulphurs are allotropes, and calcite/aragonite are two forms of one compound.

q: How many parameters are needed to describe the size and shape of a unit cell?
x: A unit cell is described by three edge lengths and the three angles between them, six parameters in all. Seven is the number of crystal systems and fourteen the number of Bravais lattices.

q: cis-1,2-dichloroethene boils at a higher temperature than trans-1,2-dichloroethene, although both have the same molar mass. The reason is that:
o: The trans isomer forms hydrogen bonds
The cis isomer is polar and has dipole–dipole attractions, while the trans isomer is non-polar
The cis isomer has a higher molar mass
The trans isomer has stronger dipole–dipole attractions
x: In the cis isomer the two C–Cl dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar and its molecules attract each other by dipole–dipole forces. In the trans isomer they cancel, so only weaker forces act.

q: A drop of ink spreads faster through hot water than through cold water. This is because at higher temperature the water molecules:
o: Have greater average kinetic energy and move faster
x: Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move and mix faster and diffusion speeds up. Stronger forces or tighter packing would slow diffusion, not speed it up.

q: Calcium carbonate occurs naturally as calcite and as aragonite, which have different crystal forms. This is an example of:
x: Polymorphism is the existence of one compound in more than one crystalline form; CaCO₃ as calcite and aragonite is the textbook example. Isomorphism is the opposite idea: different compounds with the same crystal form.

q: A unit cell has all three edges equal and all three angles equal to 90°. It belongs to the:
x: Equal edges with all angles 90° define the cubic system (e.g. NaCl). Tetragonal has only two equal edges, orthorhombic has three unequal edges, and rhombohedral has equal edges but angles other than 90°.

q: Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C, while hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), with a larger molar mass, is a gas at room temperature. The main reason is that:
o: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds because the O–H bond is highly polar
H₂S is more polar than water
x: Oxygen is much more electronegative than sulphur, so O–H bonds are highly polar and water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds. These need extra energy to overcome, raising the boiling point.

q: The boiling points of the noble gases increase from helium to xenon because, down the group:
o: The atoms form stronger hydrogen bonds
Larger, more polarisable electron clouds give stronger London (dispersion) forces
The atoms become more polar and have stronger dipole–dipole forces
Covalent bonds form between the atoms
x: Noble gas atoms are non-polar, so only London forces act between them; these grow as the electron cloud becomes larger and easier to distort. Noble gases have no permanent dipoles and no hydrogen bonding, so the polarity option is the tempting slip.

q: Which isomer of C₅H₁₂ has the highest boiling point?
o: All three boil at the same temperature
x: All have the same molar mass, but the straight chain of n-pentane gives the largest surface contact between molecules and hence the strongest London forces; the compact, nearly spherical 2,2-dimethylpropane boils lowest. Assuming equal molar mass means equal boiling point is the common slip.

q: Which order of boiling points is correct?
x: From HCl to HI, London forces increase with molecular size, so boiling points rise. HF is far above all of them because its molecules are joined by hydrogen bonds. Following molar mass alone gives HF < HCl < HBr < HI, which forgets hydrogen bonding.

q: In which of these liquids are the molecules held together by hydrogen bonds?
x: Hydrogen bonding needs H attached directly to F, O or N; methanol has an O–H group. In dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃, the H atoms are on carbon, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond with one another even though it contains oxygen, which is the tempting trap.

q: At Murree, high in the hills, water boils at a temperature below 100 °C because:
o: The atmospheric pressure is lower, so the vapour pressure of water equals it at a lower temperature
The air is colder, so less heat is needed
The vapour pressure of water is higher in the hills at every temperature
Water has fewer hydrogen bonds at high altitude
x: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. At high altitude the external pressure is lower, so this is reached at a lower temperature. The vapour pressure of water at a given temperature does not depend on altitude, so that option is the trap.

q: The molar enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 100 °C is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. The heat needed to evaporate 9 g of water at 100 °C is: (H = 1, O = 16)
x: 9 g of water is 9/18 = 0.5 mol, so heat = 0.5 × 40.7 = 20.35 kJ. Multiplying the molar value by the mass in grams (9 × 40.7) gives about 366 kJ.

q: The equilibrium vapour pressure of a pure liquid in a closed container increases when:
o: More of the liquid is added at the same temperature
A container with a wider liquid surface is used at the same temperature
The space above the liquid is made larger at the same temperature
x: Vapour pressure depends only on the nature of the liquid and the temperature; raising the temperature gives more molecules enough energy to escape. Amount of liquid, surface area and the vapour space change how fast equilibrium is reached, not the equilibrium pressure, which is the common confusion.

q: A solid melts at one temperature to a cloudy fluid, which turns into a clear liquid at a higher temperature. Such substances, used in display screens of calculators and watches, are called:
x: Liquid crystals flow like liquids but keep some ordered arrangement of molecules between the melting point and the clearing point, which makes them cloudy; their response to electric fields is used in LCDs. Amorphous solids such as glass soften gradually without this cloudy stage.

q: Diethyl ether (C₂H₅OC₂H₅) and butan-1-ol (C₄H₉OH) both have a molar mass of 74 g mol⁻¹, but at 20 °C the ether has a much higher vapour pressure. The reason is that:
o: Ether molecules are heavier, so they escape more easily
Butan-1-ol molecules have weaker London forces than ether molecules
Ether molecules have no O–H group and cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, so their intermolecular forces are weaker
Ether is ionic while butan-1-ol is covalent
x: Equal molar masses mean similar London forces, but butan-1-ol molecules are also joined by O–H···O hydrogen bonds; ether has oxygen but no H on it, so it has only weaker forces, and more molecules escape. Thinking that any oxygen-containing compound hydrogen-bonds with itself is the trap.

q: Which of these is a covalent network solid?
x: In quartz each Si atom is covalently bonded to four O atoms in a continuous three-dimensional network. Dry ice and iodine are molecular solids held by weak forces between molecules, and NaCl is ionic. Picking dry ice because CO₂ has covalent bonds confuses bonds within molecules with bonds through the whole crystal.

q: A white solid melts at 80 °C, does not conduct electricity either as a solid or when molten, and dissolves in benzene. It is most likely:
x: A low melting point, no conduction and solubility in a non-polar solvent point to separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces (naphthalene is an example). Ionic solids conduct when molten, metals conduct as solids, and network solids have very high melting points.

q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does, because:
o: Solid NaCl contains molecules, which break into ions on melting
Melting turns the covalent bonds into ionic bonds
The ions are fixed in the solid lattice but free to move in the melt
x: NaCl is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in both states; in the solid they are held in fixed lattice positions, while in the melt they can move and carry charge. The conduction is by ions, not electrons, so the free-electron option is the slip.

q: Metals can be hammered into sheets without breaking because:
o: The metal atoms are joined by directional covalent bonds
Layers of positive metal ions can slide over one another while the sea of delocalised electrons keeps holding them together
Positive and negative ions in the metal repel each other when the layers move
The metal contains hydrogen bonds that re-form easily
x: In metallic bonding the delocalised electrons are not tied to particular atoms, so when layers shift the bonding continues. In an ionic crystal, shifting brings like charges together and it shatters, which is the picture the ion-repulsion option wrongly applies to metals.

q: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. This is because in graphite each carbon atom is:
o: sp³ hybridised and bonded to four others, leaving one electron free
sp² hybridised and bonded to three others, leaving one electron delocalised over the layer
sp² hybridised and bonded to four others, with no free electrons
sp hybridised and bonded to two others, with two electrons free
x: In graphite each C forms three σ bonds within a hexagonal layer (sp²); the fourth electron, in an unhybridised p orbital, is delocalised and carries current. In diamond each C is sp³ with all four electrons in σ bonds, so none are free; giving graphite sp³ mixes up the two allotropes.

q: One unit cell of the sodium chloride crystal contains, in effect:
x: Counting shared ions: Cl⁻ at 8 corners (8 × 1/8 = 1) and 6 face centres (6 × 1/2 = 3) gives 4; Na⁺ at 12 edge centres (12 × 1/4 = 3) and 1 body centre gives 4. So there are four NaCl units per cell. Six is the coordination number of each ion, which is the tempting mix-up.

q: The coordination numbers of Na⁺ in the NaCl crystal and of Cs⁺ in the CsCl crystal are:
x: In NaCl each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ ions at the corners of an octahedron; in CsCl the larger Cs⁺ sits at the body centre of a cube of 8 Cl⁻ ions. Swapping the two values is the usual slip.

q: Arrange MgO, NaF and KCl in order of increasing magnitude of lattice energy.
x: Lattice energy grows with ionic charge and with smaller ionic size. MgO has 2+ and 2− ions and is by far the largest; NaF has smaller ions than KCl, so its lattice energy is larger than that of KCl. Looking only at size and ignoring the doubled charges puts MgO in the wrong place.

q: A crystal system whose unit cell has a ≠ b ≠ c and α = β = γ = 90° is called:
x: Orthorhombic has three unequal edges all at right angles. Tetragonal has two equal edges (a = b ≠ c); monoclinic has one angle not 90°; triclinic has no angle equal to 90°. Confusing orthorhombic with tetragonal is the common slip.
